concepts.description: A country has a comparative advantage in a good it makes at a lower cost in terms of the other goods it gives up; specializing by comparative advantage lets both sides gain.

concepts.title: Container shipping
concepts.description: Malcolm McLean's 1956 container voyage showed that loading whole boxes, rather than loose cargo, made shipping far cheaper.

concepts.title: Gains from trade
concepts.description: Voluntary trade happens only when both sides expect to gain, but a country's gains are spread widely while some workers and firms lose.

concepts.title: Global supply chains
concepts.description: Many products are made from parts and services sourced in many countries, so trade statistics and single disruptions can mislead or ripple worldwide.

concepts.title: The globalization debate
concepts.description: Globalization has lowered prices and helped poor countries grow, while job losses from import competition have been concentrated in particular places.

concepts.title: Imports and exports
concepts.description: Exports are goods and services sold abroad and imports are those bought from abroad; services, including travel spending, count too.

concepts.title: Why countries make different things
concepts.description: Countries differ in resources, climate and skills, so each can make some things far more cheaply than others and trade for the rest.

concepts.title: Ricardo's wine and cloth
concepts.description: In 1817, David Ricardo showed that Portugal and England both gain by specializing and trading, even though Portugal made both wine and cloth with fewer workers.

concepts.title: The Silk Road
concepts.description: The Silk Road linked China with the West by caravan, with goods passing in stages through middlemen.

concepts.title: Dutch tulip mania
concepts.description: The 1630s Dutch tulip craze, long called the first speculative bubble, crashed in February 1637; historian Anne Goldgar found it far smaller than legend says.

concepts.title: How unemployment is measured
concepts.description: The US counts unemployment with a monthly household survey; the unemployed must lack a job, have looked for work and be available, and people outside the labor force are not counted.

concepts.title: Frictional, structural and cyclical unemployment
concepts.description: Unemployment is frictional (between jobs), structural (skills mismatch) or cyclical (caused by recession); the first two make up the natural rate.

concepts.title: Unions and collective bargaining
concepts.description: A union is an association of workers acting together to improve their conditions. It negotiates with employers through collective bargaining and can strike. About 1 in 10 US workers is a member.

concepts.title: The Flint sit-down strike
concepts.description: In 1936 and 1937, autoworkers occupied General Motors plants in Flint, Michigan, for 44 days until GM recognized their union, the United Auto Workers.

concepts.title: Compensating differentials
concepts.description: Dirty, dangerous or unpleasant jobs tend to pay more than pleasant jobs needing similar skill. Adam Smith noticed it; economists call it a compensating differential.

concepts.title: Wages as the price of labor
concepts.description: A wage is the price of labor, set in a labor market where employers demand and workers supply labor. More productive workers are in more demand, and jobs needing long training have fewer candidates.

concepts.title: The water and diamond puzzle
concepts.description: Water is vital but cheap, diamonds are nearly useless but dear. The standard explanation is scarcity: water is plentiful, diamonds are not.

concepts.title: Institutions and the wealth of nations
concepts.description: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson link prosperity to institutions: inclusive rules support growth, extractive ones enrich an elite.

concepts.title: Other explanations for rich and poor countries
concepts.description: Other economists stress geography, disease and isolation, and all explanations meet at productivity: output per worker.

concepts.title: Weimar Germany's hyperinflation
concepts.description: In 1923, Germany printed money to pay its bills until a dollar cost trillions of marks; historians debate how much reparations were to blame.

concepts.title: Yap's stone money
concepts.description: On Yap, large stone discs quarried on Palau served as money, changing owners by shared agreement without moving.

concepts.title: Zimbabwe's hyperinflation
concepts.description: In 2008, after land reforms crippled farming and the government printed money, Zimbabwe's prices doubled roughly daily until it abandoned its currency in 2009.

concepts.title: Africa across the Equator
concepts.description: The Equator nearly halves Africa, the only continent crossed by the Equator and both tropics, so its climate zones are largely mirrored north and south.

concepts.title: Africa's young population
concepts.description: About 19% of the world's people live in Africa, the youngest continent (median age about 19); Nigeria has the most people.

concepts.title: Africa, the second-largest continent
concepts.description: Africa is the second-largest continent, covering about one-fifth of Earth's land, and flat maps often undersell it.

concepts.title: Africa's great cities
concepts.description: Cairo, Lagos and Kinshasa are among Africa's largest cities; Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across the Congo River.

concepts.title: Africa's countries
concepts.description: Africa has 54 countries, more than any other continent; Algeria has been the largest since South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011.

concepts.title: The Alpide belt
concepts.description: A second great earthquake belt runs from the Atlantic through the Mediterranean and the Himalayas to Indonesia, along the Alpine-Himalayan ranges.

concepts.title: The Alps, Europe's crumpled water tower
concepts.description: The Alps are fold mountains pushed up by a fragment of the African plate colliding with Eurasia, and their water feeds rivers flowing to four seas.

concepts.title: Air cools as you climb
concepts.description: Near the surface, air cools by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m you climb, so a tall mountain stacks climates on top of each other.

concepts.title: Climbing through climate zones
concepts.description: Plant zones stack up a mountain like a trip toward the poles, as Humboldt showed on Chimborazo; trees stop at the timberline, and the zones are moving uphill.

concepts.title: The Amazon River
concepts.description: The Amazon rises in the Andes near the Pacific, flows east to the Atlantic, carries about a fifth of Earth's runoff, and drains the world's largest basin.

concepts.title: The Andes
concepts.description: The Andes run along South America's western edge through seven countries, the world's longest continental mountain range.

concepts.title: Claims on Antarctica
concepts.description: Seven countries claim parts of Antarctica, and the claims of Argentina, Chile and the United Kingdom overlap.

concepts.title: The Antarctic ice sheet
concepts.description: Antarctica is a rocky continent under an ice sheet up to 4.8 km thick that holds about 90% of the world's ice and makes it the highest continent.

concepts.title: The Antarctic Treaty
concepts.description: The 1959 Antarctic Treaty freezes territorial claims and keeps Antarctica for peace and science; the 1991 Madrid Protocol bans mining.

concepts.title: Antarctica's extremes
concepts.description: Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent: it holds the lowest measured temperature, gets so little snow it's a desert, and sends katabatic winds pouring off its ice.

concepts.title: Antipodes
concepts.description: A place's antipode is the point directly opposite it through Earth's center: opposite hemisphere, 180° of longitude away, about 12 hours off.

concepts.title: The shrinking Aral Sea
concepts.description: The Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake, shrank after its rivers were diverted in the 1960s to irrigate cotton, bringing harsher climate, toxic dust and collapsed fisheries.

concepts.title: The Arctic: an ocean ringed by land
concepts.description: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents, and sea ice floating on it covers the North Pole.

concepts.title: Arctic sea ice
concepts.description: Arctic sea ice grows to a maximum in March and shrinks to a minimum in September; the September minimum is shrinking about 12% per decade, and losing reflective ice speeds warming.

concepts.title: Most people on Earth live in Asia
concepts.description: About three-fifths of humanity lives in Asia, crowded into South Asia, eastern China and the Pacific coasts and islands.

concepts.title: Asia's regions and empty spaces
concepts.description: Asia, the largest continent, divides into East, South, Southeast, Central, West and North Asia, and much of its interior is thinly peopled.

concepts.title: How atolls form
concepts.description: A reef fringing a volcanic island keeps growing upward as the island sinks; when the island disappears, a ring of reef around a lagoon remains, as Darwin proposed and drilling confirmed.

concepts.title: Australians live on the coast
concepts.description: Most Australians live near the coast, especially the fertile east coast, beyond which the Great Dividing Range separates the cities from the Outback.

concepts.title: Australia: a dry continent-country
concepts.description: Australia is the smallest continent and one of the largest countries; except for Antarctica it's the driest continent, with a vast arid interior called the Outback.

concepts.title: What a biome is
concepts.description: A biome is a large area defined by its vegetation, soil, climate and wildlife; the five major types are forest, grassland, desert, tundra and aquatic.

concepts.title: How borders are drawn
concepts.description: Some borders follow natural features like mountains and rivers; others are straight lines such as the 49th parallel; borders drawn without regard to local communities often cause conflict.

concepts.title: The taiga (boreal forest)
concepts.description: The taiga is the largest land biome: a belt of water-saving, snow-shedding conifers across the far north.

concepts.title: Cardinal directions
concepts.description: North, east, south and west; Earth spins toward the east, so the Sun rises roughly in the east.

concepts.title: The Caribbean islands
concepts.description: The West Indies curve in a long crescent: the big Greater Antilles, led by Cuba, and the smaller Lesser Antilles.

concepts.title: The Central American isthmus
concepts.description: Central America is a narrow isthmus of seven countries linking North and South America, with a wetter Caribbean coast.

concepts.title: Climate normals
concepts.description: Climate is usually summarized as 30-year averages; NOAA updates its US normals every 10 years.

concepts.title: Climate shapes biomes
concepts.description: Temperature and precipitation decide which biome grows where, so similar climates grow similar-looking biomes, even from unrelated plants.

concepts.title: Where climate zones occur
concepts.description: Tropical climates sit near the Equator, big hot deserts about 15 to 30 degrees out, continental climates inside big landmasses, polar climates near the poles.

concepts.title: Mountains from colliding plates
concepts.description: When India hit Eurasia, neither plate could sink, so the crust crumpled upward into the still-rising Himalayas.

concepts.title: The Congo rainforest
concepts.description: The Congo Basin holds the world's second-largest rainforest; bonobos live only south of the Congo River.

concepts.title: The Congo River
concepts.description: The Congo crosses the Equator twice, so part of its basin is always in a rainy season and it flows steadily; only the Amazon carries more water.

concepts.title: Continents by size
concepts.description: Asia is the largest continent and Australia the smallest.

concepts.title: The Continental Divide
concepts.description: A ridge along the crests of the Rockies and the Andes separates rivers that flow to the Pacific from those that flow to the Atlantic side.

concepts.title: Continental drift and Pangaea
concepts.description: Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents were once joined in Pangaea; the idea was accepted once plate tectonics explained the motion.

concepts.title: Coordinates and 0°, 0°
concepts.description: A latitude and a longitude together fix one spot; the point 0°, 0° lies in open ocean in the Gulf of Guinea.

concepts.title: Corals are animals
concepts.description: Corals are animals: tiny polyps that build limestone skeletons and live in partnership with food-making algae.

concepts.title: Coral bleaching
concepts.description: Corals stressed by warm water expel the algae that feed and color them, turning white; prolonged bleaching kills them, and climate change is the reef's greatest threat.

concepts.title: The Coriolis effect
concepts.description: Earth's rotation deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.

concepts.title: Hurricane, typhoon or cyclone
concepts.description: The same storm is called a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone depending on the ocean where it forms.

concepts.title: The International Date Line
concepts.description: The date line roughly follows the 180° meridian; crossing it westward moves the calendar a day ahead.

concepts.title: The Dead Sea
concepts.description: The Dead Sea lies more than 400 m below sea level, Earth's lowest land, and is so salty that swimmers float.

concepts.title: Ocean dead zones
concepts.description: Nutrient runoff from farms and cities feeds algae; when they die and decompose they use up oxygen, creating dead zones such as the one off the Mississippi every summer.

concepts.title: Deciduous forests and autumn
concepts.description: Winter makes water scarce, so deciduous trees shed their leaves; autumn yellows appear when chlorophyll breaks down and reveals hidden pigments.

concepts.title: Deserts are defined by dryness
concepts.description: A desert is defined by very little precipitation, not by heat, so icy Antarctica is the largest desert and the Sahara the largest hot one.

concepts.title: How deserts form
concepts.description: Deserts form under belts of dry sinking air around 30° to 35° N and S, and in the rain shadows of mountains.

concepts.title: Evidence the continents were joined
concepts.description: Matching coastlines, matching rock layers and fossils like Mesosaurus show Africa and South America were once joined.

concepts.title: Earth's metal core
concepts.description: The core is iron and nickel: a liquid outer core that makes the magnetic field and a solid inner core, revealed by earthquake waves.

concepts.title: Crust and mantle
concepts.description: Earth's thin rocky crust sits on the mantle, a thick layer of solid rock that flows very slowly over long periods.

concepts.title: Earth's connected systems
concepts.description: Earth works as connected systems of rock, water, air, life and ice (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere, cryosphere) that constantly interact.

concepts.title: What causes earthquakes
concepts.description: Stuck plate edges build up force until rock suddenly slips along a fault, sending out seismic waves from the hypocenter.

concepts.title: Earthquake magnitude
concepts.description: Each whole step in magnitude means about 32 times more energy; the largest recorded earthquake was magnitude 9.5.

concepts.title: Elevation and contour lines
concepts.description: Heights are measured above sea level, and contour lines join points of equal elevation; close lines mean steep ground.

concepts.title: Equal-area maps
concepts.description: Equal-area projections show the true relative sizes of places but distort their shapes.

concepts.title: The Equator
concepts.description: The Equator is 0° latitude, halfway between the poles, splitting Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

concepts.title: Landforms carved by erosion
concepts.description: Waves carve caves, arches and sea stacks; wind shapes rock and dunes; glaciers widen valleys.

concepts.title: Europe, a peninsula of Eurasia
concepts.description: Europe is the western peninsula of Eurasia, bounded by the Urals and three bodies of water, and itself a peninsula of peninsulas.

concepts.title: Europe's four physical regions
concepts.description: From north to south Europe falls into the Western Uplands, the North European Plain, the Central Uplands and the Alpine Mountains.

concepts.title: The Rhine and the Danube
concepts.description: The Rhine runs from the Alps to the North Sea and the Danube from the Black Forest to the Black Sea; a canal now links them.

concepts.title: Where water vapor comes from
concepts.description: Most water vapor evaporates from oceans and other open water, plants add more by transpiration, and a molecule stays aloft only about 10 days.

concepts.title: Everest's sea-floor summit
concepts.description: The rock at Everest's summit is limestone from an ancient sea floor, full of marine fossils, lifted by the collision.

concepts.title: How much land feeds us
concepts.description: Almost half of the world's habitable land is farmed, and more than three-quarters of that farmland goes to livestock, which supply under a fifth of calories.

concepts.title: Five named oceans, one world ocean
concepts.description: The Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic are named regions of one connected global ocean; the Southern is the newest named.

concepts.title: Forced displacement
concepts.description: At the end of 2024, 123.2 million people were forcibly displaced; most stayed inside their own countries, and most refugees are hosted by neighbouring countries.

concepts.title: How little water is fresh
concepts.description: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is ice or groundwater; lakes and rivers hold a tiny fraction.

concepts.title: Scarce fresh water
concepts.description: Almost all of Earth's water is salty ocean, and most fresh water is locked in ice, so usable fresh water is a scarce resource.

concepts.title: Lakes dug by ice
concepts.description: Massive glaciers scoured and deepened old valleys in the middle of North America, making the basins the Great Lakes now fill.

concepts.title: How glaciers form and flow
concepts.description: Glaciers form where snow survives year after year and is squeezed into ice; they flow slowly downhill under their own weight.

concepts.title: Earth is warming
concepts.description: Burning fossil fuels has raised carbon dioxide by more than 50%, and Earth has warmed about 1°C, mostly because of human activity.

concepts.title: How GPS finds you
concepts.description: A receiver turns signal travel times into distances and needs four satellites: three for position, one to fix its clock.

concepts.title: The GPS constellation
concepts.description: At least 24 GPS satellites with precise clocks broadcast one-way signals of their position and time.

concepts.title: How the Grand Canyon was carved
concepts.description: The land was lifted into the Colorado Plateau, then the Colorado River cut down through it over the last 5 to 6 million years.

concepts.title: The canyon's rock record
concepts.description: The Grand Canyon exposes layers of rock with the oldest, nearly 2 billion years old, at the bottom and younger layers above.

concepts.title: Grasslands
concepts.description: Grasslands grow between forest and desert on the rainfall scale; fire, drought and grazing keep them open, and grass regrows from its base.

concepts.title: The Great Barrier Reef
concepts.description: The world's largest coral reef system stretches more than 2,000 km off northeastern Australia, built by colonies of tiny animals called polyps.

concepts.title: The Great Lakes
concepts.description: Five lakes, Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario, hold about a fifth of the world's surface fresh water and drain east to the Atlantic.

concepts.title: The Great Plains
concepts.description: East of the Rockies, the Great Plains form a dry, windy grassland that slopes gently down toward the east.

concepts.title: The Great Rift Valley
concepts.description: East Africa is being pulled apart as the Somali plate separates from the Nubian plate; the Red Sea is a rift the sea already flooded.

concepts.title: The green Sahara
concepts.description: About 11,000 years ago a wobble in Earth's axis pushed monsoon rains north and the Sahara held lakes, rivers and grasslands before drying out.

concepts.title: The greenhouse effect
concepts.description: Greenhouse gases trap some of the heat Earth gives off; without them Earth would average about -18°C.

concepts.title: Groundwater and aquifers
concepts.description: Groundwater fills pores and cracks in rock and soil, like water in a sponge; usable amounts sit in aquifers reached by wells.

concepts.title: Persian Gulf oil
concepts.description: The Persian Gulf countries hold about half the world's proved crude oil reserves, formed from ancient marine life.

concepts.title: Water scarcity and desalination
concepts.description: The Middle East and North Africa have very little fresh water, so Gulf countries desalinate seawater using their oil and gas.

concepts.title: The Hadley cell
concepts.description: A loop of air: rising and raining at the Equator, sinking and drying near 30 degrees, returning as the trade winds.

concepts.title: How the Himalayas rose
concepts.description: India collided with Asia 40 to 50 million years ago; the crust crumpled upward, lifting ancient seafloor to Everest's summit, and it is still rising.

concepts.title: The abode of snow
concepts.description: The Himalayas' snow and glaciers feed great rivers, including the Indus, the Brahmaputra and the Ganges.

concepts.title: Hokulea's 1976 voyage
concepts.description: In 1976 the canoe Hokulea sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti with no instruments, showing that Polynesians could have settled the Pacific by deliberate voyages.

concepts.title: Hotspots
concepts.description: Some volcanoes, like Hawaii's, form over a stationary hotspot in the mantle, far from plate boundaries.

concepts.title: Hurricane season
concepts.description: Hurricanes feed on warm tropical water, so the Atlantic season runs June to November and peaks in September, when the ocean is warmest.

concepts.title: Ice-age sea level
concepts.description: In the last ice age so much water was frozen on land that sea level fell by about 120 m, uncovering the Beringia land bridge between Asia and North America.

concepts.title: Earth's two ice sheets
concepts.description: Only Greenland and Antarctica have ice sheets today; together they hold over 68% of Earth's fresh water, and melting Antarctica would raise the sea about 58 m.

concepts.title: Iceland's rift
concepts.description: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, and over a hotspot.

concepts.title: International migrants
concepts.description: About 304 million people, 3.7% of the world or 1 in 27, were international migrants in 2024; the United States hosts the most.

concepts.title: Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak
concepts.description: Kilimanjaro, a volcano about 3° south of the Equator, rises 5,895 m and is the highest point in Africa.

concepts.title: The Köppen climate groups
concepts.description: Köppen's system, built on vegetation zones, sorts climates into five groups: tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar.

concepts.title: How lakes form
concepts.description: Lakes fill inland basins; glaciers dug most of them, and rifts in the crust dug others, like Baikal, the deepest and oldest lake.

concepts.title: Plateaus, valleys and deltas
concepts.description: Three common landforms: raised flat plateaus, valleys carved by rivers and glaciers, and deltas built at river mouths.

concepts.title: Language families
concepts.description: A language family is a group of languages descended from one ancestor; Indo-European, from Proto-Indo-European, spans most of Europe and much of South and Southwest Asia.

concepts.title: Latitude
concepts.description: Latitude measures distance north or south of the Equator, from 0° to 90°, along parallel lines.

concepts.title: Longitude and the prime meridian
concepts.description: Longitude measures distance east or west of the prime meridian through Greenwich, chosen in 1884, from 0° to 180°.

concepts.title: Longshore drift
concepts.description: Waves usually meet the beach at an angle, setting up a current parallel to shore that carries sand along the coast.

concepts.title: How a compass works
concepts.description: A compass needle is a magnet that lines up with Earth's magnetic field.

concepts.title: Magnetic north vs true north
concepts.description: The North Magnetic Pole is not the Geographic North Pole and drifts; the angle between them is magnetic declination.

concepts.title: The major world religions
concepts.description: In 2020 Christians were about 29% of the world, Muslims about 26%, the unaffiliated about 24%, Hindus about 15% and Buddhists about 4%; Muslims grew fastest.

concepts.title: Every flat map distorts
concepts.description: A round Earth can't be flattened without distortion, so every flat map sacrifices some accuracy that a globe keeps.

concepts.title: The Mediterranean climate
concepts.description: Hot, dry summers and cool, wet winters, found around the Mediterranean and at about 30 to 45 degrees latitude on western coasts.

concepts.title: The Mediterranean, a sea that connected peoples
concepts.description: The Mediterranean sits between Europe, Africa and Asia, and ancient seafarers settled all around it.

concepts.title: Megacities and the largest cities
concepts.description: A megacity has 10 million or more people; there were 33 in 2025. By the UN's 2025 count, Jakarta, Dhaka and Tokyo are the largest, and rankings depend on how a city is measured.

concepts.title: The Mercator projection
concepts.description: Mercator's 1569 map keeps compass bearings straight for navigation but inflates areas far from the Equator.

concepts.title: The Tigris, the Euphrates and Mesopotamia
concepts.description: Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, is fertile but dry, so farming there relied on irrigation from the rivers.

concepts.title: The Mexican Plateau
concepts.description: Mexico's heartland is a high plateau between two Sierra Madre ranges, its largest and most densely populated region.

concepts.title: Volcanoes of Mexico and Central America
concepts.description: Mexico and Central America sit where several plates meet, so volcanoes like Parícutin and Citlaltépetl are common.

concepts.title: The Middle East
concepts.description: A loosely defined region centered on Southwest Asia, often including Egypt; much of it is desert, including the Rub' al Khali sand sea.

concepts.title: Why people migrate
concepts.description: People migrate because of push factors (war, food shortages, floods) and pull factors (jobs, better climate, food supply), within a country or across borders.

concepts.title: The Mississippi River
concepts.description: The Mississippi runs from a wadeable stream at Lake Itasca to a vast delta on the Gulf of Mexico.

concepts.title: The Mississippi's watershed
concepts.description: The Mississippi and its tributaries drain all or part of 31 states and two Canadian provinces, about 40% of the continental US.

concepts.title: Monsoons
concepts.description: Seasonal wind reversals driven by land heating faster than ocean; South Asia's summer monsoon brings most of India's rain.

concepts.title: The Nile's yearly flood
concepts.description: Each summer the Nile's flood spread dark, fertile silt over Egypt's fields, giving the land its name, Kemet, until the Aswan High Dam ended it in 1970.

concepts.title: The Nile flood and Egyptian farming
concepts.description: The Nile's annual flood left fertile silt that made farming possible in a desert, until the Aswan High Dam ended the flood in 1970.

concepts.title: The Nile and its branches
concepts.description: The Nile flows north to the Mediterranean; the White and Blue Niles meet at Khartoum, and the Blue Nile brings most of the water and silt.

concepts.title: North America's reach
concepts.description: North America stretches from near the North Pole almost to the Equator, and takes in Canada, the US, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and Greenland.

concepts.title: North America's shape
concepts.description: North America has an ancient rock core (the Canadian Shield), old worn mountains in the east, younger taller mountains in the west, and flat plains between.

concepts.title: New Zealand's volcanoes and geysers
concepts.description: In the North Island the Pacific Plate slides under the Australian Plate; melting rock feeds volcanoes like Ruapehu and heats water for the geysers and hot springs of Rotorua and Taupo.

concepts.title: New Zealand's plate boundary
concepts.description: New Zealand straddles the Australian and Pacific plates; in the South Island they meet along the Alpine Fault, pushing up the Southern Alps.

concepts.title: The deep-ocean conveyor belt
concepts.description: Deep currents are driven by density: cold, salty water sinks, keeping a slow global loop moving that takes about 1,000 years.

concepts.title: How deep the ocean goes
concepts.description: The ocean averages about 3,700 m deep, and its deepest point, Challenger Deep, is about 11 km down: deeper than Everest is tall.

concepts.title: Oceans by size
concepts.description: The Pacific is the largest ocean, bigger than all land combined; the Arctic is the smallest.

concepts.title: High islands and low islands
concepts.description: Pacific islands are either high volcanic islands built by eruptions or low coral islands, often atolls ringing a lagoon.

concepts.title: The Pan-American Highway
concepts.description: A road network runs from Alaska to the tip of Argentina, broken only by the Darién Gap between Panama and Colombia.

concepts.title: Permafrost
concepts.description: Permafrost is ground frozen for at least two years; only a thin top layer thaws in summer, so meltwater is trapped and the tundra turns soggy.

concepts.title: Plate boundaries
concepts.description: Plates pull apart at divergent boundaries, push together at convergent ones and slide past each other at transform boundaries.

concepts.title: The polar circles
concepts.description: The Arctic and Antarctic Circles, at about 66.5°, mark where the Sun stays up or down for a full day at least once a year.

concepts.title: Polar opposites
concepts.description: The Arctic is ocean ringed by land and Antarctica land ringed by ocean; the high, ocean-less South Pole is far colder, and the two poles take turns with six months of sunlight.

concepts.title: Where people live
concepts.description: People are spread unevenly: about 60% live in the Asia-Pacific region, India is the most populous country, and about 87% live north of the Equator.

concepts.title: Air pressure makes wind
concepts.description: Air flows from high pressure to low pressure; uneven heating by the Sun creates the pressure differences.

concepts.title: Rain shadows
concepts.description: Mountains force moist air up, so the windward side gets rain and the leeward side is left dry: a rain shadow.

concepts.title: Why rainforests teem with life
concepts.description: Year-round sunlight and moisture let rainforests hold more than half of the world's species on a small slice of the surface.

concepts.title: Reefs: crowded cities of the sea
concepts.description: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean but hold nearly a quarter of its species, in clear, warm, sunlit tropical water.

concepts.title: Coral bleaching
concepts.description: Water that is too warm makes corals expel their algae and turn white; they can recover if the heat eases, or die if it lasts.

concepts.title: Where religions are practiced
concepts.description: Religions are unevenly spread: most Muslims, nearly all Hindus and nearly all Buddhists live in the Asia-Pacific region, and sub-Saharan Africa now has the most Christians.

concepts.title: The resource curse
concepts.description: Countries rich in natural resources often grow more slowly than resource-poor ones, partly through conflict over resources; Botswana is a noted exception.

concepts.title: Where resources are found
concepts.description: Natural resources are unevenly spread: Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves and the Democratic Republic of the Congo mines most of the world's cobalt.

concepts.title: The rift and human origins
concepts.description: The Rift Valley yields key early human fossils such as Lucy, and its datable volcanic ash layers let scientists date them.

concepts.title: The Ring of Fire
concepts.description: A belt of plate boundaries around the Pacific holds about 75% of Earth's volcanoes and 90% of its earthquakes.

concepts.title: River valleys and the first civilizations
concepts.description: Many of the earliest civilizations grew up in river valleys, where water and fertile soil made farming and irrigation possible.

concepts.title: The longest rivers
concepts.description: The Nile, about 6,650 km, is usually ranked longest, but the Amazon (at least 6,400 km) disputes it because experts disagree on where rivers start and end.

concepts.title: The rock cycle
concepts.description: Any type of rock can become any other; limestone becomes marble and granite becomes gneiss under heat and pressure.

concepts.title: The three kinds of rock
concepts.description: Igneous rock cools from molten rock, sedimentary rock forms from pressed layers, metamorphic rock is changed by heat and pressure.

concepts.title: The Rocky Mountains
concepts.description: The Rockies run some 4,800 km from northern Canada to New Mexico, the best-known range of the western mountains.

concepts.title: Russia and Siberia
concepts.description: Russia is by far the largest country; most Russians live in its European part, while Siberia covers most of the land.

concepts.title: Russia's eleven time zones
concepts.description: Russia is so wide that it spans 11 time zones, and its longest railway crosses eight of them.

concepts.title: The Sahara, largest hot desert
concepts.description: A desert is defined by low precipitation; the Sahara is the largest hot desert (Antarctica is the largest overall), and most of it is rock and gravel, not sand.

concepts.title: Why some lakes are salty
concepts.description: Rivers carry dissolved salt from rocks; a lake with no outlet loses water only by evaporation, so its salt builds up, as in the Dead Sea.

concepts.title: Savannas
concepts.description: A savanna is a hot, seasonally dry grassland with scattered trees; the largest are in Africa, and fire keeps the trees in check.

concepts.title: Seas and oceans
concepts.description: Seas are smaller parts of the ocean, usually partly enclosed by land; the Sargasso Sea is the one exception, bounded only by currents.

concepts.title: The seven continents
concepts.description: Earth's land is commonly divided into seven continents; Antarctica is the only one with no permanent population.

concepts.title: Africa's shrinking mountain ice
concepts.description: Glaciers near the Equator on Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya are retreating; Kilimanjaro has lost more than 85% of its summit ice since 1912.

concepts.title: South America's countries
concepts.description: South America has 12 independent countries plus French Guiana; Brazil covers about half the continent, and Ecuador is named after the Equator.

concepts.title: South America's shape
concepts.description: South America is broad in the north and tapers south, with the Andes in the west, the Amazon basin in the north, plains in the east and center, and Patagonia in the south.

concepts.title: South Asia's landscapes and people
concepts.description: The Indian subcontinent has three great units, the Himalayas, the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the Deccan plateau, and India is now the most populous country.

concepts.title: How many countries?
concepts.description: The UN has 193 member states and 2 observer states, but lists of countries differ because places like Kosovo and Taiwan are not UN members.

concepts.title: The crops that feed the world
concepts.description: Just 15 crops give 90% of the world's food energy, and rice, maize and wheat give two-thirds of that; rice, mostly grown in Asia-Pacific, feeds almost half of humanity.

concepts.title: Subduction makes volcanoes
concepts.description: Where one plate is pushed beneath another, the sinking rock helps make magma that rises and erupts.

concepts.title: The Suez Canal
concepts.description: The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean and Red Seas without locks, separates Africa from Asia and lets ships skip sailing around Africa.

concepts.title: Sun angle and heating
concepts.description: Sunlight arrives more directly near the Equator and spreads over larger areas toward the poles, so the tropics get the most energy; tilt, not distance, drives the seasons.

concepts.title: Surface currents carry heat
concepts.description: Winds drive surface currents, which carry warm water from the Equator toward the poles; the Gulf Stream warms northwestern Europe.

concepts.title: Tectonic plates
concepts.description: Earth's outer shell is broken into rocky plates that carry continents and oceans and move a few centimeters a year.

concepts.title: Thunderstorms and lightning
concepts.description: Thunderstorms need moisture, unstable air and lift; lightning heats air so fast it expands into thunder.

concepts.title: Time zones
concepts.description: Because Earth turns 15° an hour, the world uses 24 standard time zones counted from Greenwich, with borders bent to follow countries.

concepts.title: Tornadoes
concepts.description: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air from a thunderstorm to the ground; the US has the most.

concepts.title: The trade winds
concepts.description: Steady easterly winds near the Equator, bent by the Coriolis effect, that once carried sailing ships to the Americas.

concepts.title: How tropical cyclones work
concepts.description: Tropical cyclones feed on warm ocean water, spin because of the Coriolis effect, and weaken over land.

concepts.title: Tropical rainforests
concepts.description: Tropical rainforests grow in the tropics, warm and wet all year, and are built in four layers from sunny emergents to the dark forest floor.

concepts.title: The tropics
concepts.description: The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, at about 23.5° N and S because of Earth's tilt, bound the only zone where the Sun is ever directly overhead.

concepts.title: How tsunamis travel
concepts.description: Tsunamis race across deep ocean as low waves, then slow and grow tall in shallow water; the sea may pull back first.

concepts.title: How tsunamis form
concepts.description: Undersea earthquakes lift or drop the seafloor, shoving the whole water column and launching a tsunami.

concepts.title: The tundra
concepts.description: The tundra is cold, treeless land of low plants, found beyond the Arctic Circle and high on mountains.

concepts.title: Uluru and the Anangu
concepts.description: Uluru is sacred to its Aboriginal Traditional Owners, the Anangu; the park was handed back in 1985 and the climb closed in 2019.

concepts.title: Uluru, the rock
concepts.description: Uluru rises 348 m from the Outback plain, is only the tip of a much bigger buried slab, and gets its red color from rusting iron.

concepts.title: Why cities grow
concepts.description: Cities grow as people move in from the countryside for jobs and opportunities; they began to boom with industrialization in the 18th century.

concepts.title: How volcanoes form
concepts.description: Magma rises because it is lighter than solid rock and erupts as lava, mostly near plate boundaries where sinking plates melt.

concepts.title: The water cycle
concepts.description: Water circulates between ocean, air and land, lifted by the Sun's energy and pulled back by gravity, while the total amount stays about the same.

concepts.title: Earth is mostly water
concepts.description: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, so ocean, not land, dominates the planet.

concepts.title: Watersheds and river flow
concepts.description: A watershed is all the land draining to one outlet; the Amazon's is the world's largest, and it carries about a fifth of the water running off Earth's surface.

concepts.title: Waves wear coasts away
concepts.description: Wind-made waves carry energy to the coast, carving arches that collapse into sea stacks, which erode away in turn.

concepts.title: Polynesian wayfinding
concepts.description: Polynesian navigators found their way without instruments by the rising and setting points of stars, ocean swells, homing seabirds and clouds over islands.

concepts.title: Weather vs climate
concepts.description: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere; climate is the long-term average weather of a place.

concepts.title: Weathering and erosion
concepts.description: Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion carries it away. Water is the main agent, as the Grand Canyon shows.

concepts.title: What a wetland is
concepts.description: A wetland is land where water covers or saturates the soil for at least part of the year; marshes are grassy, swamps are woody.

concepts.title: Wetlands store and clean water
concepts.description: Wetlands soak up floodwater like sponges and release it slowly, and filter sediment, pollutants and nutrients like kidneys.

concepts.title: Wetlands and wildlife
concepts.description: Wetlands are homes and nurseries for a large share of wildlife: over a third of US threatened and endangered species live only there.

concepts.title: The world's languages
concepts.description: Humans speak more than 7,000 languages, at least 40% of them endangered; English and Mandarin Chinese are the only ones with over a billion speakers.

concepts.title: How world population grew
concepts.description: World population took until about 1800 to reach 1 billion, passed 8 billion in 2022 as lifespans lengthened, and is now growing more slowly.

concepts.title: The Yangtze, the Long River
concepts.description: Asia's longest river runs from the Tibetan Plateau to the East China Sea through China's granary.

concepts.title: The Yellow River
concepts.description: Named for its loess silt, the Yellow River is the cradle of Chinese civilization and 'China's Sorrow', flowing above its plain between levees.

levels.title: Art History in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the big eras of art from cave paintings to today.
levels.summary: The oldest known art is a hand stencil at least 67,800 years old, far older than writing. Art then moved through big eras, Stone Age to modern, each answering the last.

cards.headline: The oldest known artwork is a hand. It's at least 67,800 years old.
cards.body: Someone on Muna island, in Indonesia, pressed a hand to a cave wall and blew red ochre over it. Lift the hand away and its outline stays on the bare rock. It's still there. Art history starts with that hand, and this level runs from there to today.

mascot.line: Art had a 22-hour head start on writing. Honestly, that explains why pictures still say it faster.

cards.fact: If all of art history were one day, writing wouldn't show up until after 10 p.m.
cards.context: Squeeze the 67,800 years since that hand into 24 hours. Writing, invented about 5,200 years ago, appears just after 10 p.m.: for more than 22 hours, people made art but wrote nothing down. The Mona Lisa, begun about 1503, arrives about 11 minutes before midnight. Most of art's story happened before anyone could write about it.

events.label: Hand stencils, cave animals, carvings
Egypt, Greece, Rome: Egypt's art serves king and gods
Western art is mostly art for the church
Italy revives ancient Greece and Rome
Drama, movement, emotion
Painters break the old rules

cards.headline: Every era answers the one before
cards.body: Eras aren't just labels; they talk to each other. Renaissance is French for "rebirth": starting in 14th-century Italy, artists revived the ideas of ancient Greece and Rome. Centuries later, photography could record the world exactly, so painting no longer had to. Modern painters, starting in mid-1800s France, threw out the old rules. Each new era is partly a reply to the last one.

levels.title: What Counts as Art?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why people have disagreed about what counts as art.
levels.summary: In 1926 US customs taxed Brancusi's Bird in Space as metal because it didn't look like a bird. In 1928 a court ruled it art: art could express an idea, not just copy nature.

cards.headline: In 1926, US customs decided a famous sculpture wasn't art. Just metal.
cards.body: So they taxed it like any factory-made object. The fight that followed went all the way to court, where a judge had to settle a question people still argue about in galleries: what counts as art?

cards.headline: A bird with no wings
cards.body: The sculpture was Constantin Brancusi's Bird in Space. Picture a tall, slender strip of bronze, polished like a mirror. Brancusi left out the wings and feathers, stretched the body long and shrank the head and beak to a slanted oval. It doesn't show what one particular bird looks like. It's about the idea of flight.

cards.headline: Two ideas of art collide
cards.body: Customs followed the old rule: a sculpture was carved or shaped in the likeness of natural models, like people and animals. No likeness, no sculpture. So they charged a 40% duty on it as a manufacture of metal. Brancusi's side said art could capture an idea instead. The critic Frank Crowninshield testified that it suggested flight, grace and speed, just as a bird does.
cards.callout: Old test: does it look like something? New test: does it express something?

mascot.line: Next time someone says "my kid could make that", remember: that argument once needed a judge.

cards.fact: In 1928, a court ruled that Bird in Space was art.
cards.context: The court noted a new school of art whose artists tried to portray abstract ideas rather than imitate natural objects, and said it had to be recognized. The ruling even admitted it might be hard to associate the thing with a bird. It was still pleasing to look at, and a work of art. The idea of art had moved, and the law moved with it.

questions.explanation: The court recognized a new school of art that portrays abstract ideas rather than imitating natural objects.

options.label: It copies a bird more exactly than a photo can

options.rationale: It breaks with realism, like modern painters did.

levels.title: The Artist's Toolkit
levels.objective: After this level you can name the basic elements of art: line, shape, color, texture and space.
levels.summary: Every artwork is built from the elements of art: line, shape, color, texture and space (many lists add form). Even empty space has a shape.

cards.headline: Every picture ever made uses the same few building blocks.
cards.body: A cave wall, a comic, the icon on your phone: artists build them all from what they call the elements of art. Learn five of them and you can take any picture apart.

cards.headline: Line and shape
cards.body: Start with line: a mark longer than it is wide. It can be straight or curved, thick or thin. Close a line into a loop and you have a shape. Shapes are flat and come in two families: geometric, like squares and circles, or organic, the free-form shapes you find in nature. A smiley face is one circle, two dots and a curve. Line and shape, doing all the work.

mascot.line: I once tried to pet a painted porcupine. Very smooth. Mildly embarrassing.

cards.headline: Color and texture
cards.body: Color is light reflected off things (Level 4 is all about it). Texture is how a surface feels, or looks like it would feel. It can be real, like thick paint you could touch, or only implied. A drawing of a porcupine can look prickly, but run your finger over it and the paper is smooth. The prickles are an illusion.

cards.fact: Empty space has a shape too.
cards.context: Space is the area around and between things. The empty part is called negative space, and it has a shape of its own: think of the hole in the letter O. Space also means the feeling of depth, when a flat picture seems to open up like a window. That's the five: line, shape, color, texture and space. Many lists add form, meaning 3D shapes like balls and boxes.

levels.title: How Color Works
levels.objective: After this level you can explain primary and complementary colors and how artists use them.
levels.summary: Newton bent the spectrum into a color wheel. Red, yellow and blue are the painter's primaries; complements sit opposite, look more intense side by side, and mix to brown.

cards.headline: In 1824, the royal tapestry works in Paris had a problem: weak colors.
cards.body: The new head of dyeing at the Gobelins, a chemist named Michel-Eugène Chevreul, went looking for bad dye. He found something much stranger. To see what, you need a color wheel.

cards.headline: Newton bends the rainbow
cards.body: In his book Opticks, in 1704, Isaac Newton took the colors of the spectrum and bent them into a circle: an early color wheel. Painters use the idea to this day. Three colors sit at the heart of a painter's wheel: red, yellow and blue, the primaries. Every other color is a mix of them. Mix two primaries and you get a secondary: orange, green or violet.

cards.headline: Opposites on the wheel
cards.body: Colors directly across the wheel from each other are complementary: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet. Each pair shares no primary. Red is a primary, and green is blue plus yellow, so between them they use all three. Mix complements in paint and they cancel each other out into brown.
cards.callout: Red ↔ green · Blue ↔ orange · Yellow ↔ violet

mascot.line: So if a color looks off, check the neighbors before you blame the paint.

cards.fact: A color changes depending on its neighbors.
cards.context: That was the Gobelins mystery. The dye was fine; the colors woven next to each other were changing how each one looked. Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839. Put complements side by side and each makes the other look more intense. His ideas went on to influence painters, including the Impressionists.

levels.title: The First Artists
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the oldest known cave art and how it was made.
levels.summary: The oldest finds go from lines (a 73,000-year-old ochre crosshatch at Blombos Cave) to hands (stencils blown in ochre) to scenes (a picture story at least 51,200 years old in Sulawesi).

cards.headline: The oldest known drawing looks like a hashtag.
cards.body: It's a crosshatch of red lines on a small flake of stone from South Africa, about 73,000 years old. The earliest finds tell a story in three steps: first lines, then hands, then whole scenes.

cards.headline: Step 1: lines
cards.body: The flake comes from Blombos Cave. Someone drew on it with a pointed crayon of red ochre, an earth pigment that gets its color from iron oxide. It's at least 30,000 years older than any other known drawing. Is it art? Researchers still disagree. The lines might mean something, or they might just be left over from sharpening the crayon.

cards.headline: Step 2: hands
cards.body: Remember Level 1's hand, at least 67,800 years old? To make a stencil, you press your hand to the rock and blow pigment over it, sometimes through a pipe. Lift your hand and its outline stays. On Muna island, someone later went back and narrowed the fingers, turning a human hand into something closer to a claw.

mascot.line: Three figures and a pig. Honestly, better plot than some movies I've seen.

cards.fact: The oldest known picture story is at least 51,200 years old.
cards.context: On a cave wall at Leang Karampuang, also in Sulawesi, three human-like figures interact with a wild pig. It's not one animal on its own: it's a scene, the earliest known narrative art. Its age comes from thin mineral crusts that formed on top of the paint, dated by the uranium in them.

levels.title: Lascaux and Chauvet
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the animal paintings in the caves of Lascaux and Chauvet.
levels.summary: Lascaux (about 17,000 years old) has huge black aurochs and closed in 1963 after visitors harmed it. Chauvet (about 35,500 years old) is full of lions, rhinos and mammoths.

cards.headline: In 1994, cave explorers in France felt a faint draft from a pile of stones.
cards.body: Behind it was a cave sealed by rockfalls for at least 21,000 years. On its walls: cave lions, woolly rhinos and mammoths. But first, meet an older discovery: Lascaux.

cards.headline: Lascaux: the Hall of the Bulls
cards.body: Four teenagers found Lascaux in 1940. Radiocarbon dating of its charcoal says about 17,000 years old. In its most famous room, four huge black bulls (aurochs) sweep across the rock, some about 5 meters long. Their bodies are drawn from the side, but their horns twist toward you, so you see both at once. The painters built scaffolding to reach the ceiling.

mascot.line: Sometimes the kindest way to love a painting is to stop breathing on it.

cards.fact: Lascaux lasted about 17,000 years in the dark, then about 15 years of tourists.
cards.context: It opened to visitors in 1948, up to 100,000 a year. Their traffic and the artificial lights faded the colors and brought algae, bacteria and crystals. In 1963 it closed. Since 1983, visitors have toured a replica nearby instead.

cards.headline: Chauvet: twice as old
cards.body: Radiocarbon dates put most of Chauvet's art at about 35,500 years old, roughly twice Lascaux's age. Its artists chose dangerous animals: among over 400 animals of 14 species are cave lions, woolly rhinos, mammoths and bears. They scraped walls clean, strengthened outlines and smudged charcoal to shade. In the End Chamber, a pride of lions hunts bison.

levels.title: The First Sculptures
levels.objective: After this level you can describe early carved figures and what they may have meant.
levels.summary: The Lion-Man, carved in mammoth ivory about 40,000 years ago, mixes lion and human. Small figures of women, like Hohle Fels and Willendorf, have unknown meanings.

cards.headline: About 40,000 years ago, someone carved a creature nobody had ever seen.
cards.body: It stands upright like a person, but it has the head of a cave lion, and it's carved from a mammoth's tusk. Meet the Lion-Man.

cards.headline: The Lion-Man
cards.body: He was found in Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in Germany and stands 31 cm tall, about the length of a school ruler. That makes him the largest known sculpture of Ice Age art. When a modern experimenter carved a copy with Ice Age-style stone tools, it took hundreds of hours. That's a lot of time to spend on something you can't eat, wear or hunt with.

cards.headline: Small women, carved to hold
cards.body: The Venus of Hohle Fels, from another German cave, is mammoth ivory, 6 cm tall and 35,000 to 40,000 years old. Instead of a head, she has a small pierced loop, so she may have been worn as a pendant. The Venus of Willendorf, found in Austria, is about 30,000 years old: 11.1 cm of limestone, tinted with red ochre. She has no face at all, only a pattern like a braid or a cap.

cards.fact: "Venus" isn't their name, and nobody knows what they meant.
cards.context: Modern scholars borrowed the name from the Roman goddess of love, a goddess from many thousands of years later. Ideas about Willendorf include a fertility figure, a good-luck charm and a mother goddess. And a 2022 study added a travel story: her stone likely came from near Lake Garda in northern Italy, across the Alps.

levels.title: Stonehenge and Great Stones
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what monuments like Stonehenge show about early societies.
levels.summary: Stonehenge took hundreds of workers, stones from Wales and feasts drawing people from across Britain. Göbekli Tepe, about 11,500 years old, was built by hunter-gatherers.

cards.headline: Stonehenge's builders joined giant stones the way a carpenter joins wood.
cards.body: Picture a ring of huge upright stones on a grassy plain, with stone beams laid across their tops. The beams are slotted on with joints you'd normally find in furniture. Monuments like this tell you who built them: how many people, how organized, and what mattered to them.

cards.headline: Built by hundreds, over centuries
cards.body: Stonehenge began as a circular ditch and bank about 3000 BC; the stones went up about 2500 BC. The giant sarsens, about 25 tons each on average, came from about 25 km away. The smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales, more than 200 km away. Moving, shaping and raising them took hundreds of people. That's not a weekend project. That's a society working together.

cards.fact: Some pigs at Stonehenge-era feasts came from as far as north-east Scotland.
cards.context: At Durrington Walls, near Stonehenge, archaeologists have found over 38,000 animal bones. Pig teeth show animals raised in west Wales, northern England and north-east Scotland, then slaughtered at midwinter. Stonehenge itself is lined up with the Sun: at midsummer the sun rises beside the Heel Stone, and at midwinter it set through the tallest arch. People came from far away, at special times of year.

cards.headline: Göbekli Tepe: older than farming
cards.body: In southeastern Turkey, hunter-gatherers began Göbekli Tepe about 11,500 years ago, more than twice Stonehenge's age and before farming. Its T-shaped limestone pillars reach over 5 meters and weigh up to 50 tons. Some are carved with foxes, scorpions and lions. Others have arms and hands carved down their sides, meeting in front over a belt: giant stone people. Building together may have led people to settle, not the other way round.

levels.title: Why Early People Made Art
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the main ideas about why early humans made art.
levels.summary: Why early people made art is debated. Main ideas: an urge to record the world, hunting magic (with a reindeer problem), a spirit world, and keeping records.

cards.headline: Nobody left a note explaining the cave paintings.
cards.body: So researchers work from clues, and they disagree. The purpose of this art is still debated. Here are the main ideas. Hold them as ideas, not answers.

cards.headline: Idea: because people need to
cards.body: One view skips usefulness altogether: humans have a basic need to record and recreate the world around them. On this view the first artists drew for the same deep reason you doodle in a meeting. The catch is that it's hard to test.

cards.headline: Idea: hunting magic
cards.body: Maybe painting an animal was a kind of spell, to make a hunt succeed or herds multiply. It has a big problem at Lascaux. The bones left behind show the painters mostly ate reindeer, yet reindeer are almost absent from the walls. If you're casting a spell for dinner, you'd paint dinner.

mascot.line: Notice the word "may". In this level, it's doing a lot of honest work.

cards.headline: Idea: a spirit world
cards.body: Most experts think cave art was symbolic or religious, sometimes both. One version: shamans entered trances to contact spirits, and the art shows that other world. Mixed creatures fit this idea, like Level 7's Lion-Man, or the Muna hand narrowed into a claw, which researchers think may reflect links between people and animals, or spiritual beliefs.

cards.fact: Some marks may be records, not pictures.
cards.context: Researchers suggest the patterns on an engraved ochre plaque from Blombos Cave may be a way of counting or storing information. Others wonder whether animals painted in their seasonal coats worked as an early calendar. The ideas don't have to compete: one cave could be a gallery, a temple and a notebook.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The First Artists
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the earliest known art and the main ideas about why it was made.
levels.summary: Radiocarbon dates charcoal back to about 50,000 years; uranium-series dates crusts over mineral paint, giving a minimum age. That's why records say 'at least'.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: how do you date a painting nobody signed?
cards.body: Every date in this chapter came from a lab, not a label. Here's the whole chapter in order, then how those numbers were found, and why so many of them start with "at least".

events.label: An ochre crosshatch at Blombos Cave
A hand stencil on Muna island
The Lion-Man, carved in ivory
Chauvet's lions and rhinos
Lascaux's great aurochs
Stonehenge's stones go up

cards.fact: Charcoal is a clock.
cards.context: Radiocarbon dating measures carbon-14 in things that were once alive, like the burnt wood in charcoal, and works back to about 50,000 years. Many of Chauvet's black lines are charcoal, so labs can date the drawings themselves: most are about 35,500 years old. At Lascaux, charcoal from the cave gives about 17,000.

mascot.line: "At least 67,800 years" is science being honest. The hand might be older still.

cards.headline: Why "at least"?
cards.body: Red ochre is iron oxide, a mineral, and many paintings have no organic material to date. So researchers date something else: thin mineral crusts that grew over the paint, using uranium, as at Leang Karampuang. The crust formed after the painting, so the paint must be older. That's a minimum age. The real one could be older, which is why records keep getting broken.

levels.title: Mesopotamia
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Mesopotamian art, from stepped temples to carved seals.
levels.summary: Mesopotamian cities raised stepped mud-brick ziggurats, like Ur's for the moon god Nanna, and carved tiny stone cylinder seals that printed pictures on clay.

cards.headline: The first cities built their temples out of mud.
cards.body: Mesopotamia is Greek for "between rivers": the land of the Tigris and Euphrates, where the world's earliest civilization grew up. Its builders worked in brick, and its artists often worked in something humbler still: clay. This level runs from a temple tower down to a picture about the size of your thumb.

cards.headline: A staircase for a god
cards.body: A ziggurat is a stepped temple tower. Picture a stack of ever-smaller brick platforms, like a giant wedding cake. The core was mud brick, wrapped in a tougher skin of baked brick. The best known, at Ur, went up about 2100 BCE under King Ur-Nammu for the moon god Nanna. Three staircases led up, and on the flat top sat a temple. The tower's whole job was to lift that temple up.

mascot.line: Carving a picture backward, in stone, the size of a thumb. Suddenly neat handwriting seems easy.

cards.fact: A cylinder seal prints a whole picture strip in one roll.
cards.context: Carve a design into a small stone cylinder, often no bigger than 5 cm tall, about the size of your thumb. Roll it across wet clay and the carving comes out raised, as one continuous band, the way a patterned paint roller works. Scholars count these tiny carvings among Mesopotamia's finest art.

cards.headline: A signature you could roll
cards.body: Seals weren't just decoration. Rolled onto clay, a seal marked what you owned or made a document legally binding: rolled on a tablet, it showed you had authorized the text, like a signature. Remember Level 1's writing, about 5,200 years ago? It was Sumerian cuneiform, wedge-shaped marks pressed into soft clay with a stylus. In Mesopotamia, words and pictures shared the same wet clay.

levels.title: The Rules of Egyptian Art
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the rules that kept Egyptian art so consistent for 3,000 years.
levels.summary: Egyptian artists drew each body part from its most complete angle, used a shared 18-unit grid, and made important people bigger. The style held for about 3,000 years.

cards.headline: Egyptian art kept one look for about 3,000 years.
cards.body: It did change, slowly, but it held its character so well that you can spot Egyptian art from across a museum. The secret is rules. Learn three and you can read almost any Egyptian painting.

cards.headline: Rule 1: every body part at its best angle
cards.body: Stand like a figure in an Egyptian painting and you'd need a very flexible neck. The head is in profile, but the eye looks straight at you. The shoulders face front, while the legs walk sideways. This wasn't clumsiness: artists combined viewpoints to show each part of the body in its most complete form. Level 6's aurochs did something similar, with bodies from the side and horns turned toward you.

mascot.line: Egyptian painters were using graph paper long before it was homework.

cards.fact: A standing figure measured 18 squares from the soles of the feet to the hairline.
cards.context: Artists laid a grid on the wall first, so a body came out with the same proportions whatever its size. Why stop at the hairline? Crowns and headdresses varied, so the top of the head didn't count. Every workshop sharing one grid is part of why the style stayed so steady.

cards.headline: Rule 3: bigger means more important
cards.body: In a tomb painting, the king or the tomb owner towers over everyone. His family is smaller, his servants smaller still. It isn't distance; it's rank. Remember Level 1: Egyptian art served the king and the gods, and size told you at a glance exactly who mattered.

levels.title: Art for the Afterlife
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Egyptians filled their tombs with art.
levels.summary: Egyptians believed the ka, a life force, needed food forever, and that images could magically provide it. So tombs held painted food, models like Meketre's and shabti workers.

cards.headline: In 1920, archaeologists opened a room nobody had entered in almost 4,000 years.
cards.body: It was in the tomb of Meketre, an Egyptian official. Robbers had stripped the tomb long ago, but they missed one small hidden chamber. Inside, packed tight, stood 24 painted wooden models. Why would anyone bury a miniature world?

mascot.line: Bread that never runs out and never goes stale. Egyptian tomb painters were very practical dreamers.

cards.headline: Food for the ka
cards.body: Egyptians believed each person had a ka, a life force that still needed food and drink after death. Real offerings run out. Pictures don't. So tombs were filled with scenes and models of food and food-making, which could feed the ka forever without ever being used up. A painted loaf is the one snack that never goes stale.

cards.headline: Meketre's model estate
cards.body: Meketre's models show boats, people carrying offerings, and workshops where craftsmen work and cooks make bread and beer. They look like toys. They weren't. Egyptians believed images could magically give the dead safe passage to the afterlife and food once there. Every tiny baker had a job: keep Meketre fed.

cards.fact: Some tomb figures were buried to do your chores.
cards.context: Shabtis were small figures of substitute workers, placed in tombs so they could do the dead person's labor in the afterlife. That fits the Egyptian dream: not a distant paradise, but daily life on Earth carried on, without the pain. Tomb art showed people as they wished to stay forever, which is why the tomb itself was called the ka house.

levels.title: Greek Vases
levels.objective: After this level you can explain black-figure and red-figure vase painting.
levels.summary: Black-figure (Corinth, about 700 BCE) painted black figures and scratched in details. Red-figure (Athens, about 530 BCE) flipped it and painted details with a brush.

cards.headline: A Greek jar from about 540 BCE reads like a comic strip.
cards.body: The Greek heroes Achilles and Ajax sit facing each other, playing a dice game. Words run from their mouths: Achilles calls "four", Ajax calls "three". The painter, Exekias, signed it as both potter and painter. His figures are black on orange-red clay, and that color scheme is the key to this level.

cards.headline: Black-figure: paint the shape, scratch the detail
cards.body: Black-figure began in Corinth about 700 BCE, and Athens took it up by the end of the 7th century BCE. The painter filled in each figure in glossy black on the bare clay, then scratched fine details through the black with a sharp point. Think of scratch art, on a vase. Exekias's dice game is black-figure.

cards.fact: The black on a Greek vase isn't paint. It's clay.
cards.context: Painters used slip, a fine liquid clay. The color change happened in the kiln, in a three-stage firing that switched between letting air in and shutting it out. The slip came out glossy black, and the bare clay returned to orange-red. The painter had to picture the finished colors before the fire made them.

mascot.line: Same clay, same kiln, same black. Just swap which part gets painted, and a whole art form changes.

cards.headline: Red-figure: the big flip
cards.body: In Athens, about 530 BCE, painters reversed the whole system. Now the background was painted black, and the figures were left in bare red clay. Details went on with a brush instead of being scratched. That small switch mattered: a brush curves and flows, so painters had more freedom to show bodies, movement and facial expressions. Red-figure went on to dominate.

levels.title: Greek Sculpture
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Greek sculptors moved from stiff figures to lifelike bodies.
levels.summary: Archaic kouroi stood stiff and frontal, in a pose reflecting Egypt. Just after 480 BCE the Kritios Boy shifted his weight onto one leg: contrapposto. Polyclitus then wrote the rules.

cards.headline: For generations, Greek statues stood at attention. Then one relaxed.
cards.body: Try it: stand with your weight on one leg, like you're waiting for a bus. Your hips tilt, your shoulders tilt the other way, and you look alive. Greek sculptors had to discover that.

cards.headline: Archaic: the kouros
cards.body: From about 615–590 BCE, Greek sculptors carved kouroi: stone statues of standing young men, some used as grave markers. Picture one facing straight ahead, left foot slightly forward, arms close to his sides, fists clenched. If he reminds you of Egypt, that's no accident: the kouros reflects Egyptian traditions, especially their body proportions. Remember Level 12's grid?

mascot.line: Next time you lean on one leg in a queue, congratulate yourself. You're doing classical sculpture.

cards.headline: The Kritios Boy shifts his weight
cards.body: Just after 480 BCE, a marble youth from the Athenian Acropolis did something new. He rests his weight on his left leg, while his right leg relaxes, bent at the knee. That's contrapposto: one leg takes the load, so the hips, shoulders and head tilt. Weight on both legs looks like a statue. Weight on one looks like a person.

cards.fact: The Spear Bearer was a rulebook you could walk around.
cards.context: About 450–440 BCE, the sculptor Polyclitus made the Doryphoros, or Spear Bearer, to illustrate his book, the Canon, on the ideal proportions of the human body. His relaxed contrapposto helped free Greek sculpture from rigid, face-front poses. The stiff kouros had become a body at ease, measured to an ideal.

levels.title: Greek Temples
levels.objective: After this level you can name the three Greek column styles and describe the Parthenon.
levels.summary: Greek columns come in three orders: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian. The Parthenon, built from 447 BCE for Athena, is the peak of Doric, full of subtle curves still debated.

cards.headline: The Parthenon looks perfectly straight. It isn't.
cards.body: Its base bulges upward in the middle and its columns swell slightly. People have argued about why since Roman times. First, though, learn to read a Greek column from the top.

items.label: Doric
points: No base; a plain, cushion-like capital
The sturdiest look

items.label: Ionic

Stands on a base; more slender

items.label: Corinthian
points: Capital carved with acanthus leaves
The most decorative

cards.headline: The Parthenon
cards.body: Built of white marble from 447 BCE and finished by 438 BCE, the Parthenon honored the goddess Athena. Its architects, Ictinus and Callicrates, worked under the sculptor Phidias, and they made it the high point of the simplest order, Doric. Simple, here, doesn't mean plain: almost nothing about this building is as straight as it looks.

mascot.line: Measure first, explain second. The Parthenon keeps both jobs busy.

cards.fact: The Parthenon's base rises about 5 cm in the middle.
cards.context: Its columns bulge slightly (entasis), and its corner columns are thicker. The classic explanation comes from the Roman architect Vitruvius: the curves correct optical illusions, so the temple looks straight. In 2026, the mathematician Alain Goriely argued there's no evidence the curves produce those illusions at all. The curves are measured fact; the reason is still an argument.

levels.title: Roman Art
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what Roman art borrowed from Greece and what it added.
levels.summary: Rome copied Greek statues and borrowed the Greek orders, then added its own: warts-and-all portraits from around 100 BCE and the Pantheon's huge concrete dome.

cards.headline: We know Level 15's Spear Bearer only because Romans copied it.
cards.body: None of Polyclitus's original statues survive. The Doryphoros is known only through Roman copies. In the late Republic, admiring earlier Greek art became the fashion in Rome. So what did Rome add of its own?

cards.headline: What Rome borrowed
cards.body: Rome also borrowed Greece's architecture. The Romans adopted the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders you met in Level 16 and adapted them for their own buildings. So far, a very good student. But Rome also pushed in directions of its own.

mascot.line: Earned the wrinkle? Rome carved the wrinkle. Every single one.

cards.headline: Warts and all
cards.body: Level 15's Greeks measured out an ideal body. Roman portrait sculptors, flowering around 100 BCE, recorded every line, crease, wrinkle and even blemish. The style is called verism. It wasn't a lack of tact: especially for men, the wrinkles of age signaled dignity and authority, the face of experience. Imagine a politician's poster that proudly adds ten years.

cards.fact: The Pantheon's dome is about 43 m across, and it's concrete with no steel inside.
cards.context: The emperor Hadrian rebuilt the Pantheon between 118 and 128 CE. Its unreinforced concrete dome was unmatched in scale until modern times. The only light comes through an opening about 8 m wide at the top, the oculus, The columns came from Greece. The dome was pure Rome.

levels.title: Mosaics
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how mosaics are made and where they flourished.
levels.summary: Mosaics are pictures of small closely set tesserae. Greeks invented cut tesserae; Romans laid mosaic floors across the empire, like Pompeii's Alexander Mosaic.

cards.headline: A Pompeii doorway still says "Beware of the dog".
cards.body: At the entrance of the House of the Tragic Poet, a black dog on a chain is set into the floor in tiny pieces of stone, above the words CAVE CANEM. Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE, and the warning survived. It's a mosaic: a picture you could walk on.

cards.headline: Pictures made of dice
cards.body: A mosaic is built from tesserae: small, closely set pieces of stone, glass, tile or shell. The name is Latin for "cubes" or "dice". The Greeks refined floor pictures made of pebbles, then invented cut tesserae, shaped to fit tightly together. Tighter pieces meant denser, more detailed pictures, the way more pixels make a sharper photo.

mascot.line: More than a million pieces, each placed by hand. And you thought a thousand-piece jigsaw was a big weekend.

cards.headline: The Alexander Mosaic
cards.body: In the House of the Faun, another Pompeii house, lay a floor about 5.8 m wide, made around 100 BCE from more than a million tesserae. It shows Alexander the Great fighting the Persian king Darius III at the Battle of Issus. Scholars believe it's a Roman copy of a lost Greek painting. If so, a great Greek painting survives only as a Roman floor.

cards.headline: Floors of an empire
cards.body: Roman mosaics spread throughout the empire as floor decoration. The same art covered a guard-dog warning at a front door and a great battle in the House of the Faun. Across the empire, Romans walked on pictures.

levels.title: Early Art of China and India
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Terracotta Army and early Buddhist sculpture.
levels.summary: About 8,000 clay soldiers, each with its own face, guard China's first emperor. In India, early art showed the Buddha only as symbols, until about the 1st century CE.

cards.headline: In 1974, farmers digging a well in China found an army.
cards.body: Underground stood about 8,000 life-size soldiers made of clay, buried to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of a unified China, who died in 210 BCE. Meanwhile in India, sculptors faced the opposite puzzle: how do you show someone without showing him?

cards.headline: An army of individuals
cards.body: The soldiers weren't made in one piece. Each was assembled from separately fired sections, then given its own detailed face. Picture thousands of clay men, each with a face of his own. Their weapons, cast from an unusual metal alloy, are still shiny and sharp today. Their job: guard the emperor's tomb.

cards.headline: The Buddha as an empty seat
cards.body: At Sanchi, in India, stone gateways added to the Great Stupa in the 1st century BCE are crowded with carved stories of the Buddha's life. But look for the Buddha himself and you find only signs: a wheel, an empty throne, a pair of footprints. The story is all there; the star never appears. It's like a film where the hero is always just off screen.

mascot.line: A Buddha dressed a bit like a Roman emperor. Art history loves a surprise guest.

cards.headline: Then the Buddha got a face
cards.body: Around the 1st century CE, sculptors in two places, Gandhara and Mathura, each began showing the Buddha in human form. Gandhara, in today's northwestern Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan, made a version you might recognize: a youthful, Apollo-like face and robes like those on Roman imperial statues. Greek and Roman ideas had traveled a very long way.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Ancient Worlds
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the art of Egypt, Greece, Rome and early Asia.
levels.summary: Ancient statues were painted (polychromy): colors found with infrared and ultraviolet light, mostly lost to weather and air, and flaking in minutes off the Terracotta Army.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: the ancient world wasn't white.
cards.body: Picture a Greek statue and you probably see bare white marble. Its makers wouldn't recognize it: Greek and Roman statues were once painted in bright colors. First, the chapter in order. Then, where all that color went.

events.label: Ur's ziggurat rises for the moon god
